Miss AGNES C. MACPHAIL (Grey-Bruce): I rise to a question of privilege. My attention has been called to a statement alleged to have been made-it is in quotations-by Premier Hepburn, appearing in the Ottawa Journal of June 2, at page 11, in which, discussing compensation for the family of Constable John Lewis, who was slain by Norman "Red" Ryan in Sarnia on May 23, Mr. Hepburn, the Premier of Ontario, is reported to have said:
We are not involved in any way. He was let out of the penitentiary because he was the "pet" of R. B. Bennett, Senator Mullins and Miss Agnes Macphail. We had nothing to do with paroling the man.
Oh, oh.

I do not believe that anyone really thinks this is funny, for it undoubtedly had most unfortunate consequences, resulting as it did in the death of Constable John Lewis. I have borne a good deal of

adverse criticism about my activities in relation to penitentiaries, and in this matter I thought I ought to make it clear so far as I am concerned. I did not intercede on behalf of Norman "Red" Ryan. I asked Mr. Gallagher, chief of remission service, whether he would go through the files and give me a statement, which I should like to put on Hansard. I have received from him the following letter dated June 6, 1936:
Dear Madam:
Complying with your request, I have had the departmental records very carefully examined to ascertain 'whether you had, at any time, intervened, or asked for clemency on behalf of Norman, or "Red" Ryan.
As a result of our diligent search. I may definitely assure you that we have found no trace whatever of any communication from you in this case.
Yours respectfully.
M. E. Gallagher,
Chief of Remission Service.
I have no desire to blame anyone or to say anything further; I simply wish to make it perfectly clear to the house and the country that at no time did I intercede on behalf of Norman Ryan.
I would like to make this statement in this connection-
Order.

subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext: I am sorry that I cannot follow my right hon. friend at all.

subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext: Well, the present government appoints four directors, and that gives them eight votes, and they promulgate a policy that meets with the approval of the existing governor and deputy governor: that gives them ten votes. But another administration holds an entirely different view.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext: Another government?

subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
Yes, another administration. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) has formed a government, and it has an entirely different conception of the functions of the central bank. Then, obviously, the will of the people would be thwarted by this organization. The argument which was made the other day in connection with the national railways has far greater force if applied to this situation than it had with reference to the railway. You have here four men, with eight votes, plus the two that come to the governor and deputy governor as members of the board and not directors, making ten in all, as against a possible seven. Whereas the other side of the picture might be this, that the governor and the deputy governor together with the seven would make nine, as against eight. That position might easily arise because the present governor and the deputy governor are appointees of the government; in future the board of directors will elect their own governor, but his appointment is subject to the approval of the governor in council. Therefore, while in law the government does not appoint, in fact, by withholding approval until someone is elected by the directors of whom the government of the day approves, it does appoint. I am pointing out that the contingency which was indicated with such force the other day respecting the period during which men hold office in another branch of the public service has much greater strength when applied to this case, because the two who control are not directors but are members of the board; they have not votes as directors, but they have votes as nominees of the directors, and they are the governor and the deputy governor. So you have a contingency here on either side. You have either the combination of the governor and deputy governor with your

seven private-interest directors, making nine in all, as against eight votes represented by the four government-named directors, or e con-verso, you have the two and the eight votes, making ten, that would thwart any effort made by those elected by the other shareholders to give effect to their policies. I submit that is not what the government intends, because it is the very negation of the plan that was unfolded by the minister, and it does not give that democratic control of the organization to which reference was made. In other words it permits, on the one hand, men to thwart the will of an incoming government, or it permits those who have been appointed to hold office to thwart the will of those who may be elected by private interests-if such it should be called-the seven elected by the shareholders.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext: I grasp clearly now what is in my right hon. friend's mind: I did not grasp it previously. After all the issue is a rather simple one. Pictured as my right hon. friend pictures it, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and others sharing his views on monetary matters-I am not at all clear that they are revolutionary, but I am assuming my right hon. friend viewed the problem as involving a revolutionary change-

subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext: Not revolutionary.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
In the sphere of monetary matters. I do use the word "revolutionary" not from the standpoint of force but in its economic sense; that, I believe, is what he has in mind.
The statement of the right hon. gentleman is that in such an event under the new set-up of the Bank of Canada it would be possible that the board of directors might be able to defy the government of the day. Of course there is only one answer to that argument, the answer I endeavoured to give the other day. The parliament of Canada, the House of Commons of Canada, must be supreme. Undoubtedly if such a contingency arose the government of the day, being unable to secure the carrying out of the policies which it believed it had a mandate from the people to cariy out, would come before parliament and ask for such amendments to the law as would enable it to carry out its policies. In my opinion, Mr. Chairman, they would have a perfect right to do so. The people'of this country have a right, I believe, to get that which they vote for in the way of major policies of that description, and I would fully expect that if the bank as constituted at the time such a change in parliamentary representation took place was not responsive in broad, great matters, major matters of

Bank oj Canada
economic policy, to the will of the then existing parliament, the then existing government would come forward with proposals for the amendment of this law which would ensure the will of parliament being carried out.
I distinguish very carefully, Mr. Chairman, between that and the day to day conduct and functioning of the bank, which indeed is nine-tenths of its work. I do not assume that there will be a clear, marked division of view between one director and another because one happens to represent the shareholders and another happens to represent the government or between either of those two classes and the governor or deputy governor. I believe that in the day to day conduct of the business of the bank these men, being men of substance, men whom I believe to be as patriotic as any of the rest of us, will sit down together just as any other body of men would and endeavour so to administer the affairs of the bank as to give the maximum of service to the people of Canada, in accordance with the trust imposed upon them by this parliament. In practice I do not think they will be in those watertight compartments of divided view suggested by the right hon. leader of the opposition. After all, the discussion on this bill has had much more to do with what should be done with the bank than with the actual nature of the amendment itself. When I sav what should be done with the bank perhaps even that is wrong; perhaps I should say what should be done by the bank in the exercise of that all important function to which I made reference in detail in introducing the financial resolution. Any differences of opinion that exist in this house are with respect to what are the proper and sound functions of the bank in relation to our economic set-up in Canada. That is the point, and that point, I anticipate, will bring about a divergence of view for many years to come.
Later on I shall expand a little on the views of the government with respect to bank policy, but I am sure no one here would expect me to indicate that the bank is going to inflate or that it is going to deflate. How would it be possible to carry on the regulatory functions if I were to make such an announcement? The announcement to-day of a policy of inflation inevitably would be followed by a degree of wild speculation which undoubtedly would leave ruin in its trail, which could not be prevented by any agency that I know of as long as people are free to buy from and sell to each other either commodities or securities. No, Mr. Chairman, the functioning of this bank is a matter of day to day regulation of the volume of cash and credit at the disposal
of the Canadian people in order to enable them to discharge their ordinary trading functions with each other. To the extent that the amount of credit and cash is increased, to that extent money is made easier. To the extent to which it is decreased, to that extent money is made tighter. To those who say the bank has been following a policy of deflation I can only enter a complete denial. The facts and figures themselves absolutely prove that such is not the case. As we go along with the bill I shall present further details which I think will tend to prove my statements in this regard.
With regard to the board itself, and to come back to the point now before the committee, the government deems it of importance not merely that government policy, broadly speaking, should control the functioning of the bank. That we deem all important, but we also deem it important that there should be provision for voices, other than voices appointed by the government, to be heard in connection with the business of the bank. That really is the whole point. Shall there be any provision for other government appointees having any voice at all? We believe that to be all to the goods, and such experience of other central banks as I have been able to gather indicates that there is some merit in not relying completely upon a board composed solely of government appointees in connection with such an important function as the one we are now discussing. Government control is essential, in our view, but the voice of business generally, if you like, as represented in this case by the shareholders, is also of importance. It is not as though the shares could be monopolized by a few. That is not possible. The average holding, if my memory serves me aright, is only between nine and ten shares. Surely there is an advantage in bringing to the board a voice which is not the voice of the government, while at the same time retaining absolute control from the point of view of government policy. In spite of what the right hon. leader of the opposition says I firmly believe that that balance is brought about by -what we have before the committee. After all the difference between us is very small. My right hon. friend does not regard the governor and the deputy governor as being directors within the meaning of this act.

subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext: The statute says they are not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
The statute says they are not. That is correct, but the statute also says that they vote at directors' meetings and it is in terms of votes that the will of the

Bank oj Canada

directors is expressed. While the statute may say that they are not directors, for my purpose if the statute says they vote that is quite sufficient, and in terms of the expression of view by way of votes the figures will be as I gave them the other day. At the outset there will be ten votes of government appointees as compared with seven votes of the elected members of the board, ultimately working out in 1940-41 and thereafter to six votes of government appointees and three votes of appointees by the shareholders. After all what we want to look to is the ultimate, and the six to three position is the one we will attain within a measurable time. Those six votes are composed of four directors appointed by the government of the day and the governor and deputy governor. Even taking my right hon. friend's measurement of the matter, by 1940-41 the permanent constitution of the bank will be four direct government appointees, apart from the governor and deputy governor, as against three appointed by the shareholders. In addition, however, on what might be called the government side of the fence are the governor and deputy governor, making up the total of six votes.
I have given a good deal of thought to the manner in which we may expect this set-up to work out within the limits I stated a few moments ago, of the policy of the government having absolute government control but with other voices being heard. I should like to be able to set this directorate upon a very high plane of public service. It would be my desire, and I know it would be the desire of the government, to make the directorate of this institution the blue ribbon of recognition in Canada of probity, character, sound judgment, and reputation. It ought to be one of the highest ambitions of a Canadian to become a director of the Bank of Canada and thus have a direct voice in the handling of that great function to which I referred in introducing the resolution, the function of regulating the volume of credit and currency in this country, in order that it may meet the public needs of Canada.

Every piece of legislation drafted by the late government is impossible to understand, and I congratulate the Minister of Finance upon being able to understand some part of it. It is a discovery! Every piece of legislation-I emphasize the word "every"-that has been put on the sta-

tute books during the last five years is a maze and is amazing. It is amazing to think how obscure can be the mind of certain law makers. That is to be regretted; for every citizen of this country should know the law; no one is excused for ignorance of the law. The man who has no legal knowledge, the man on the street, looks at the shelves filled with these statute books and asks: What is that library? Is that the Eliot library? Is that an encyclopaedia? It is an encyclopaedia of half-baked knowledge. It is the statutory legislation of the late government.
Sir, first and always I have been opposed to a central bank. I said it at the time the legislation was enacted, but I accept the views of the majority of the members of my party;
I stand by them. In my humble view the majority of the members should decide the policy of the party. But this does not prevent my saying that every piece of legislation passed by the late government was an obstacle in the way of progress. Why was it passed? Because the right hon. gentleman, the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Beamett) in spite of his knowledge from encyclopaedias, could not concentrate on finance and explain it in plain language to the house and to the country; and moreover each of his colleagues, from the oldest to the youngest, did not know a word about finance. They may be rich, but leaving their wealth aside who would go to them for advice?

speechtext:
I am talking about the
sponsors of the first bill, those who studied it in council but brought no illumination to the house, and who now make little distinctions about a word here and a word there. Sir, when you wear stockings, after a certain time they need to be mended. If you wear them longer they need more mending, until at last you give them to the poor. Here is need for a lot of mending. Why not give the Bank of Canada to the poor and dispense with the mending?
I have the highest regard for the Minister of Finance, who is much more experienced and has much more lucidity of mind than his predecessors in office during the last five years, including the fifth year. From confederation until a few years ago the Minister of Finance was the big boss of finance in this country. He could make the banks tremble. He was the guardian of the wealth of the country. But on account of the weakness of the late government it was decided

Bank oj Canada
by them to call for supermen to look after the finances of this country, and we had this central bank act. Sir, we must go back to fundamentals. We must have a simplification of the law in order that the law may be understood by everyone. The legislation should be just as clear to every citizen as the traffic regulations, with signs here and there to show the way, to indicate curves in the road. This legislation has been brought down on account of the incompetency of former ministers of finance who were afraid to take the responsibility for what they had to decide, and who practised inflation in no small degree when they increased the price of gold and passed legislation affecting the holdings of insurance companies. When we think of the way our finance has been in a mess during the last five years, the Minister of Finance deserves every good wish in his efforts to restore it, in spite of the bad legislation with which he has to deal in order to accomplish that purpose.
Will you. please, Mr. Chairman, tell the hon. member for Calgary West to keep his remarks to himself and let me proceed with my own? He is disturbing the order of this committee.

speechtext: How about the bill?

Coming back to fundamentals, it has been shown during this session that the banks have deposits to the same amount as they had five years ago. Therefore there is as much money now as there was then. Why, then, does it not circulate? Because of the lack of confidence brought about by the previous administration. It is now improving. But what counts is not only the amount of currency kept as deposits in the banks, but also the clearings. When the former government came into power the clearings fell by $5,000,000,000 a year. Imagine, sir: in a small country like this the clearings of the banks in 1930 were $20,000,000,000. an amount two-thirds as large as the public debt of the United States, which is a richer country than ours and in which there are many more people. It means that the people of Canada were trading together. But after that administration came into power the amount fell by $5,000,000,000, due to the lack of confidence of the people in that government. That is a matter of public knowledge; it must be known to hon. gentlemen of the Tory party. Yet, sir, having destroyed confidence in the hearts and minds of Canadian citizens, they presume to instruct us! They say: There should be so many directors; the directors should do this and that, "according to my own knowledge." It is ridiculous. It is 12739-222J
absurd. The first thing necessary to restore confidence is for those so-called geniuses to keep their mouths shut, and then remove themselves gently from the picture. Think of this, sir: those who enjoyed the protection of the late government, one of whom has now built a house outside of Canada, who was chairman of the investment committee of the Sun Life Assurance Company, and who, when his own bank refused to lend money to his companies, invested the money of the insurance company of which he was one of the leaders in his own business, and after everything went down in a mess, the date government gave a fictitious par value to all the stock that was held by that insurance company. That is what happened; it is known to every member of this house. My hon. friend from Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps) must admit that I am speaking to the question now.

As I have done before. Mr. Chairman, I shall not insist upon it, but I stand by what I have said. The majority of my Liberal colleagues in this house have decided to support this legislation, and I am ready to stand by them. On the other hand, the present Minister of Finance occupied his present high position some years ago, and with success. He had a very pleasant budget to submit to the country at that time. I wonder why he should not be given the responsibility that he formerly had as minister in charge of the Department of Finance.
The hon. member for Calgary West has spoken about democratic control. If the Minister of Finance has the same authority and the same powers that he had five years ago under the statute in force at that time we would have real democratic control through the Minister of Finance. Because of these birds of prey that have caused so much damage in the banking business the Minister of Finance should be armed with the criminal code and should see to it that every one, no matter how highly he may be placed in 'our social life, should be treated according to his dealings. Then we would have democratic control. The present Minister of Finance is competent to accomplish these high functions, and in that way we would get rid of that mess of legislation which paralyzes the country, and at the same time confidence would be restored and the clearings would reach higher and higher levels. It is very simple. It may not be accepted because it is simple. Some people remind me of the fellow who put a riddle to another man. He said, Tell me what looks like an egg, is round, contains a yelk and white, has a" shell,

and barks." The other fellow could not guess it, so the first one told him, "It is an egg." The other man said, "An egg does not bark." "No," said the other man, "that was to make the puzzle more difficult." Every piece of legislation of the previous government was like that. It was always to make the life of the country harder and more difficult, and I ask on behalf of my countrymen in all provinces of Canada that we may have a simplification of legislation in order that the Canadian people may understand something of the law of the land.

My understanding of the resolution as it appeared on the order paper, and certainly it has been my understanding right along, was that the directors to be appointed by the government should have control of the board of directors. The resolution as it passed the house read in part:
... and to provide for election and appointment of directors in such manner as to assure voting control of the board by directors appointed by the government.

speechtext: We are doing just that.

subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
Even at the end of the time of expiration of the present directors' terms of office there will be six votes, as it were, of directors appointed by the government, including the governor and deputy governor, and three by directors representing the shareholders. The three votes, with those of the governor and deputy governor, make five, while the directors appointed by the government would only have four. On the other hand, however, if the governor and deputy governor were satisfied to vote with the directors representing the shareholders, we would have five votes on that side and the directors appointed by the government would have only four votes.
I now refer the committee to section 9. I understood the government was taking oon-

trol so that it could determine the general long range policy of the bank. Section 9 provides that if the governor does not agree with the decision of the directors he can refer the matter to the government, which can either affirm or disallow the decision. Suppose the governor and the deputy governor, who will be elected for seven years, decide to throw in their lot for seven years with the directors representing the shareholders. That would mean that for seven years there would be no way in which the government could force the bank to carry out its wishes. The Minister of Finance has referred to parliament being supreme in these matters, but in matters of finance it seems to be that this house, and not parliament, which includes the senate, should be supreme.
If this administration decided on a certain line of policy in regard to the central bank, and the governor and the deputy governor appointed by the former government decided to take a contrary view, and could carry with them the directors appointed by the shareholders, the government would lose control over the financial policy of this country, and this house of parliament would lose control, and that is a very serious matter. The preamble of the Bank of Canada Act states that the purpose of the central bank is:
... to regulate credit and currency in the best interests of the economic life of the nation, to control and protect the external value of the national monetary unit, and to mitigate by its influence fluctuations in the general level of production, trade, prices and employment, so far as may be possible within the scope of monetary action.
Suppose we pass the bill in this form; then if it should happen that the governor and the deputy governor lined up with the directors appointed by the private shareholders, we would be putting it in the power of the senate to decide what the financial policy of this country should be in regard to the operations of the central bank. I submit that since we are not taking over one hundred per cent ownership of the bank we should make very sure that we get one hundred per cent government control. When we provide that two people, appointed by the last administration, can thwart the expressed wishes of the government in regard to monetary policy by linking up with the private shareholders; when we provide that we cannot do anything about it iunless we pass an amendment to the Bank Act which must pass the senate, then we arc not taking over control of the Bank of Canada in the complete way we should.
I ask the government to give consideration to what I have said and bring the control of this bank strictly and fully within the resolution passed by this house so that there

Bank oj Canada
may be no doubt about the question of control. I plead with them to do that at this stage. If we intend to have control of the bank, let us make sure of having control. It would not do any harm to provide for the appointment by the government of another director so that we may be sure that the government, responsible as it is to the House of Commons, shall have control of the financial policy of the Bank of Canada, that important branch of the public service, without having to go over to the other house 'to get their consent. I submit that that is the important thing, and I do plead with the government to keep the matter of control by the government beyond doubt by providing for the appointment by the government of another direotor.

Financial matters are usually so intricate and complex that the average layman, especially a farmer, has very little knowledge of them. That is the supposition, but I wish to present my views more along the lines of a business man or farmer than as an expert.
The bill before the committee has for its purpose the amending of the Bank of Canada Act, whereby the bank will be converted from a privately owned to a publicly owned and controlled bank. With that purpose I have no quarrel. I do say, however, that the method to be adopted, namely, to issue additional stock to the amount of 85,100,000 to be owned by the government, leaving the original stock of $5,000,000 in the hands of private interests, is not the proper method and is not what the public expected, based on the promises made prior to the last elections. I should like to read an extract from the Saskatchewan Farmer of May 28, as follows:
In view of the disappointment manifest in Liberal ranks in Saskatchewan over the decision of the King government not to eliminate rivate shareholders from the Bank of Canada, ut, instead, to take control of the bank by the issue of new majority stock to be owned
Bank of Canada

by the government, it is of special interest to note that the new Labour government of New Zealand is following the other plan of Ouying out the shareholders,-the plan, which was thought, by the rank and file, would be followed in Canada. Newspaper correspondents show that the Labour government has given New Zealand the clearest possible proof that it means business. Its first legislative act has been to force through parliament in less than a week a reserve bank amendment bill vesting it with powers of control over currency, credit and banking such as are possessed by no other government in the empire, and by no foreign states except Russia, Germany and Italy.
The editorial goes on to say that perhaps the plan being adopted by that government is the proper one. I am not placing my views against the views of expert members of the government, especially the Minister of Finance. This procedure may be the proper procedure, and it may provide the results that we all desire. Recently the government of France decided to make the Bank of France a publicly owned and controlled institution. The editorial to which I have referred states that the government of France intends a reform of the statutes of the Bank of France to guarantee the preponderance of national interests. The bank at present is a private institution. I will not modify my previous statement because I believe it is the intention of the government of France to get control of the bank, allowing a certain amount of private interest, along, I presume, lines similar to those taken by the government in this country. It seems to me we should profit by the experience of other countries. New Zealand embarked upon a central bank about the same time as Canada did, and after their experience they decided that a bank half private and half public was not in the interests of the nation and so they determined to make it a purely national institution. I suggest that this government-perhaps they have done so-should seriously consider the action taken by other countries and profit by their experience.
In my opinion a central bank should have the sole right to issue currency and to regulate the nations credit. It should also have the power to control the interest rates charged by financial institutions; if it cannot do that it will never justify its existence. The burden of excessive interest rates is the nation's greatest problem. If the central bank here would do what was done in England with the cooperation of the Bank of England, it would perform a useful function. In this connection I should like to read an extract from the Western Producer; to me it is the most comprehensible explanation of the action taken by Great Britain, which I at any rate

have read. The title is The Refunding of Debt. I quote:
F. S. Wright, of the tax research bureau, in a recent letter to the press, gives us some information regarding the refunding in 1932 of the British war loan. Permit me, in supplement, to quote what A. W. Kiddy, financial writer, says on the same subject in the Spectator, most orthodox of London weeklies, in the issue of February 28 last.
"The amount of the proposed conversion was 2,000 million pounds sterling. The holders of the bonds were invited to convert, voluntarily, from the existing 5 per cent to 3J per cent, and they were notified that all those who declined to convert would have their bonds paid off. Now the British government did not have the money to pay such a colossal sum. The transaction was only made possible by a potential creation of credit to the amount necessary. This was possible through the concurrence of the Bank of England. And Mr. Kiddy remarks that the creation was possible -though in fact it was not -resorted to-"and because the investor knew that it would be possible and that the effect would be to make it impossible for this vast amount of money to be reinvested without occasioning a colossal rise in security prices, general consent was given to the conversion."
There are two points to be observed. First, that the so-called "voluntary" conversion was accompanied by a veiled threat which in effect made it compulsory; "either you will do this, or it will be the worse for you." And second it affords a striking illustration of the power of credit expansion where the will is there: as Mr. Kiddy says, it "was not actual credit expansion, but a powerful expression of potential power in that direction." The effect of the transaction was beneficial, enabling a considerable burden of debt to be lifted from the taxpayer.
If one calculates it at H per cent, the amount saved to the English taxpayers on $10,000,000,000 is $150,000,000 per annum.
Now the only difference between this case and the recent experience in Alberta is that the Alberta government did not have the backing of the Bank of England. Could it have had the concurrence of the Bank of Canada if it had sought it? And the further reflection will occur to the student of finance, that if the British government had power to call two billions sterling "out of the vasty deep" of the national credit, for the purpose of debt conversion, why should it not have exercised this power for the purpose of extiction of the debt? Probably because that would not have suited the ends of the money kings. They live upon debt, lending is their business and if the British public had so simple a lesson in the possibility of wiping out of debt, the next step would have been payment of the whole of the national debt! Then what would become of the power of the Lords of Money?
This is a rather long quotation, and while perhaps my own views are not in accordance with the latter part of the statement, I have nevertheless given the whole of it, because I think that is only fair. Let us return now to Australia. Australia, realizing that it could not continue to pay high interest rates-I believe the government consulted the people

Bank oj Canada
but no results were obtained-took the matter into consideration, and the Prime Minister of Australia, in consultation with the premiers of the several states, decided to reduce the internal debt^that is, the interest-by 22i per cent. This was made compulsory, being put upon the statute books. We have therefore lessons from other countries to guide us.
We must face this issue sooner or later. The longer we delay the conversion of the public debt and the lowering of the interest rate, the greater will be the difficulties the Canadian people will have to contend with. Action in this regard in a very short time is inevitable or the result will be chaos. While, I confess, I am not a financial expert, I think it worth while to give some extracts from the observations of men who have given this subject a great deal of attention, and who no doubt know what they are talking about. I wish to quote from a speech made by the Hon. W. D. Herridge at Hamilton recently. It is published under the title, Debt must be Faced. Mr. Herridge says:
However that may be, the fact is that we are overborne by debt and that something must be done to free us from it. It cannot be absorbed by the golden rays of prosperity. It is beyond the curative powers of bigger and better business. It must be cut away. That means a serious operation. It involves more than a voluntary conversion of our national debt. It may require a revision of the whole range of vested claims. That is indeed a grave matter. But we must face it and face it without delay. We must resist the almost irresistible temptation to try by milder means to cure, in its secondary stages, that dread disease which ends in general bankruptcy. The orderly reconstruction of our undefaulted obligations upon a just and sustainable basis may well be looked upon as admirable. No one loses by it. And everyone knows that it is done pursuant only to our promise to do our best to pay.
And now I wish to quote from a speech made by the present Minister of National Defence, the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie), in 1935. At that time he was not giving the views of his party or those of the present government; he made it plain that he was expressing only his own views. This was what he said:
Sixth, I suggest the reduction of rates of interest, on all outstanding obligations in the Dominion of Canada. Seventh. I suggest a national conversion scheme reducing the interest on all internal debt to two and a half per cent. Eighth, I advocate immediate negotiations with outside nations where our external bonds are held, for a mutually satisfactory scheme for the reduction of interest on external bonds.
These are the opinions of experts and as such should receive consideration.
In my opinion one of the duties of the central bank should be to call the bondholders together and inform them that the nation
cannot continue to pay the present high rate of interest on outstanding bonds and ask for a voluntary conversion. I have sufficient faith in the Canadian people to believe that they would agree to this, but it will take a national move to bring this about. We have had provincial and municipal defaults and complaints from all over Canada, but the bondholders have merely said, "AVe cannot meet your wishes." But if the national government, with a united nation behind them, made that demand, the bondholders would come across and say "In the nation's interests we agree to have interest rates cut down." There is no doubt in the world about that. That is why I urge the present government, in the exercise of the power which they will have, to take the matter up with the bondholders and see whether we cannot secure a reduction in interest on government bonds.

I submit a nationally owned bank should have the power to regulate interest rates on all mortgages. I am deeply interested in this problem, for I know something about the real conditions. After one or more years of hardship and suffering in western Canada through crop failures, or because of crops produced at a loss, the people whom I represent in this parliament held a public meeting in the city of Portage la Prairie, and I was appointed the chairman. The object of the meeting was to impress upon the government the necessity of reducing the interest rates we had been paying, because we realized that in the end it would be impossible to meet the payments. The hall was full; we could have filled two or three halls of the same size. A committee was appointed to traverse the province of Manitoba and discuss this subject with all who would listen. I was a member of the committee. We had several meetings in various parts of the province. Finally we took the matter up through the United Farmers of Manitoba, and at their convention, held in Brandon, I suggested that a petition be circulated and presented to the Manitoba government asking them to reduce interest rates. A petition bearing thousands of names was sent to the government. They were sympathetic, but it appears that they had no power to reduce rates of interest. We did
Bank oj Canada

not get the reductions, but we got a debt adjustment act. I am very sorry it is necessary to have such legislation on the statute books of Canada, but so long as the present conditions continue we shall have debt adjustment acts and farmers creditors' arrangement acts and other legislation of a like kind to save people from eviction.
I wish to quote from Hansard of last year remarks made by a then member whose absence from this 'house is, I believe, a national calamity. I refer to Mr. Coote. I do not wish to say anything derogatory of his successor, but I knew Mr. Coote very well as one who was always fighting the battle for the common people, and I regard his absence from this house as a distinct loss to the nation. Mr. Coote told us what other countries have done with regard to reducing interest rates for farmers. He said:
In Argentine the banks have agreed to reduce interest rates two per cent to farmers.
He went on to say:
This rate is five per cent. A corresponding rate prevails on mortgages.
South Africa in 1933. The government paid one and a half per cent on farm mortgages and the farmer three and a half per cent. Any mortgage company refusing to take five per cent, a tax is levied that takes all for the state above five per cent. The amount of this tax is paid to the farmers who have paid it to the mortgage company.
New Zealand in 1932 passed the National Expenditure Act in which they reduced interest rates on farm mortgages to five per cent.
I believe that through a properly constituted central bank the government could very well compel our lending institutions to accept reasonable interest rates, the maximum of which should be, in my opinion, five per cent.
When the minister introduced his budget he told us that Canada's total investment in farm loan board loans amounted to 816,790,000. When one considers that the New Zealand government, whose population is probably less than one-third that of Canada, has $250,000,000 invested in farm loans, it must be admitted that Canada through its government has made but a very puny effort in the matter of lending money to the farmers at a low rate of interest. I believe the central bank should exercise sufficient power to lend millions upon millions of dollars at the rate of five per cent interest to farmers and others engaged in legitimate enterprise. I believe they can do it and it should be done, though only if the private lending institutions of this country refuse to do so. In my opinion all farm mortgages should be reduced to five per cent. In this connection I want to point out to the minister that farmers up until last year were 
paying interest at the rate of 6J per cent on loans froin the farm loan board. This has caused a great deal of dissatisfaction in view of the fact that the farmer who took out a loan only as recently as last year is not charged more than five per cent. I have had several letters on this subject. I think the government should consider the advisability of reducing all farm mortgages held under the board to the prevailing rate of five per cent. It would benefit not only the farmers but the government and the people in general.
I had intended to make some further observations, but the committee have been very patient in listening to my remarks and I am not going to delay them any longer. Neither from the government, the members of this house, nor the people I represent have I attempted to conceal my dissatisfaction with this proposed legislation. I believe we should have had a publicly owned and publicly controlled bank instead of the measure that has been presented to us. Nevertheless, believing as I do that the government and the Minister of Finance have the interests of our people at heart, I shall abide by their judgment and their decision and give this legislation my support.

But whether or not the province of Ontario can get funds, the fact is that there is an enormous amount of unemployment in Ontario and a great deal of work needing to be done there which is not being carried on. And across Ontario to-day steps are being taken to reduce unemployment relief, which steps are causing a general situation of unrest in that province.
Now, let me turn to Quebec. I suppose it can be said that that province is not without funds; that Montreal is not without funds. Nevertheless t'he fact remains that an unemployment situation exists in that city, and *that the men responsible for the administration of Montreal and the men responsible for the administration of the affairs of the province of Quebec are at their wit's end to find some way to meet debt and public obligations of the city of Montreal. A great many people believe the reason for that is that we have failed properly to observe our constitution, have failed to exercise properly and wisely the powers which are, by our constitution exclusively reserved to the dominion parliament. A great many people still believe we should have a properly constituted central bank that would issue currency and credit in terms of public need, to satisfy the domestic, social and industrial needs of the Canadian people. Under our constitution there is a definite responsibility upon parliament
Bank oj Canada

to maintain peace, order and good government, and in order that parliament may fulfil that duty and that function, certain legislative powers are exclusively reserved to the national parliament. As provided 'by section 91, matters reserved to the dominion parliament include:
1.	The public debt and property.
2.	The regulation of trade and commerce.
3.	The raising of money by any mode or system of taxation.
14.	Currency and coinage.
15.	Banking, incorporation of banks, and the issue of paper money.
That is the section of the British North America Act with which we are dealing in this legislation. Savings banks, weights and measures, bills of exchange and promissory notes, interest, legal tender, bankruptcy and insolvency are, under this section, also reserved to the dominion. These powers place on parliament the constitutional duty of determining, creating, issuing and sustaining the circulation of the media of exchange that will provide both government and people with a continuous circulation of adequate volume of sound and uniform currency. For that reason parliament should: (1) define the units of exchange that constitute the nation's money; (2) create the money needed to maintain national security and ordered progress; (3) regulate the volume of money created and issued; (4) stabilize the value of the unit of exchange internally and externally; and (5) regulate the circulation of money by taxation and otherwise.
We hear a lot of talk about funny money, rubber money, sound money and boloney dollar's. But I think it must be plain to any thinking man that parliament under a constitution which gives it the power to create money, to deal with every phase of law that has to do with the regulation of the monetary system, and which at the same time gives to that parliament the power to withdraw money from circulation by any mode or system of taxation, invests in that parliament the power to create and to maintain the circulation of a sufficient amount of money to preserve a decent measure of progress. Parliament can, by exercising its power to create and put into circulation money, along with its power to withdraw it from circulation, avoid all the evils, or at least all the disastrous evils, of too much or too little money in circulation. In other words, we have the constitutional power, and we should make the political attempt to avoid the evils of inflation and the disasters of deflation, which are just as bad.
Let me say that what we are doing in the matter of paper currency is in direct conflict with what parliament has already done in the

matter of coin currency. Under the power to create money, which is given us by our constitution, we create money, not by any mysterious method, but by the enactment of four laws: the Currency Act, revised statutes of 1927, chapter 40; the Depart ment of Finance and Treasury Act, revised statutes of 1927, chapter 71-and under the amendment of 1931 we have now made the mint a branch of the Department of Finance-the Bank of Canada Act which we are now amending, and which was passed in 1934; and the Bank Act,, statutes of 1934, chapter 24. What did parliament do when it passed the Currency Act? It declared the thing that the people of Canada must use for money. By section 15 of that act parliament declared that where money is involved in public or private accounts, contracts, trade or other transactions Canadian legal tender must be used. By section 2 of that act parliament has declared that the denominations of money in the currency in Canada shall be dollars, cents and mills, the mill being one-tenth of a cent and one hundred cents being a dollar. By section 17 of chapter 48 of the statutes of 1931 we made the Royal Mint, as I said a moment ago, a branch of the Department of Finance. In the administration of the mint, which is subject to the regulations which parliament under section 20 of the Currency Act has authorized the governor in council to make, legal tender coin money by section 8 is defined as follows:
(a)	in the case of gold coins, legal tender for any amount;
(b)	in the ease of silver coins, legal tender in payment for an amount not exceeding ten dollars;
(e) in the case of nickel coins, legal tender in payment for an amount not exceeding five dollars;
(d) in the case of bronze coins, legal tender in payment for an amount not exceeding twenty-five cents.
The point I wish to make is that out of what parliament has done with regard to coin money a policy has been developed which should be followed in the creation of paper currency money, because what we are doing in regard to our subsidiary coin, which is only partly legal tender money, we have more reason to do in regard to our paper currency, which is full legal tender money.
Under the provisions of section 24 of chapter 43 of the statutes of 1934, the Bank of Canada Act, Bank of Canada notes are made full legal tender money, and the Bank of Canada is authorized to create and issue these bank notes as such.
Under the powers of the Bank Act and the Currency Act we in parliament have created legal tender money.

speechtext: The hon. member will find that the chartered banks of Canada possess today millions of dollars in silver and in copper coin, and they can do nothing with these coins except to keep them in their reserves for the possible use of those who come to the bank. subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
There are some people who never use any other money than petty cash. They are not all millionaires and they are not all accustomed to using $50 bills. The great majority of our people never get any money but copper, nickel and silver coins and bills of small denominations. The money of the great masses of our people consists of copper coins, nickel coins, silver money and bills of small denominations. That is the only money they ever use.
Parliament has established as Canadian legal tender subsidiary currency token coins of little or no actual value. I hope my hon. friend will follow me here. Parliament can and does create money as a profitable function of government. Through the mint, which is now a branch of the Department of Finance, the government creates and issues metal tokens as currency which take their money value from the law which parliament has passed. Therefore, parliament creates money by passing laws. More than that, parliament creates money as a highly profitable function of government when it mints metal coins. For example, the Minister of Finance can buy an ounce of silver at forty-four cents and it can be minted into coins having a value of $1.35, with sufficient left over to pay the cost of minting. Therefore, if the government gets value for its expenditures when such money is paid out to the civil service, to contractors, or for the purchase of governmental supplies, the government makes a profit of ninety-one cents.

I do not suppose the minister has looked into the matter. The same thing applies proportionately to nickel and bronze coins. By making silver certificates legal tender and convertible info silver dollars, as has been done in the United States, the government can hold the silver coins in its vaults and issue convenient paper currency against them, get the same results and do away with the inconvenience of the carrying round of silver coins by the public.
My hon. friends talk rather glibly about the small change which they say is not important in the country, but let me give the value of that money which has actually been created by the government. Under the Currency Act and the Department of Finance, the government has created and issued silver coins up to the value of $34,210,267, nickel coins up to the value of $2,259,500, and bronze coins up to the value of $2,772,735. The total issue of subsidiary coins is valued at $39,242,502.
I should like to point out to hon. members of this committee that there has been a great change in the attitude of people and governments towards money. If we can do that with metal, we can do, and we are doing, the same thing with paper currency. I know men will say that you cannot create money without having something behind it; that you cannot create money without having a reserve into which it is convertible; that you cannot get something for nothing; there are a great many men in high positions of authority in the country who repeat these epigrams and think they are establishing a reputation of sophistication, but an examination of what this parliament is doing right now will prove otherwise.
This conclusion is confirmed by this particular bill under consideration. Section 24 of the Bank of Canada Act gives to the bank the sole right to issue Bank of Canada notes and makes them full legal tender. By the passage of the Bank of Canada Act provision was made for the repeal of chapter 41 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, the Dominion Notes Act, under which this parliament issued its own paper currency. In 1934 parliament transferred from the government to the Bank of Canada its constitutional obligation and constitutional right and duty to issue legal tender paper currency. Under section 26 of the Bank of Canada Act the gold reserves which the bank is required to hold is reduced to twenty-five per cent of the value of its notes in issue. Parliament has thus given to the Bank of Canada the power to expand $25 worth of gold into $100 worth of legal tender currency. In doing that, it

does exactly what it does when it authorizes the mint to take 26-4 cents worth of silver and mint it into a dollar. The proportion of the money value of the silver dollar to the money value of the gold dollar is almost identical with the proportion of -the money value of the gold bill to its gold reserve support.

subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS
speechtext:
It was not the League of Nations; it was the economic conference of 1933. If there is any other information that my hon. friend would like, I shall be very glad to give it to him.
In a word, parliament, by the enactment of the Bank of Canada Act, has given away its power to create and issue paper currency to the Bank of Canada. As a result, the Bank of Canada is able to print for every $100 worth of gold that it holds, $400 worth of legal tender Canadian cash with which it may purchase, among other assets, gold and interest bearing bonds printed and issued by the government. Thus we see parliament giving away its power and its constitutional duty to print paper currency to a corporation that now enjoys this power.
At the end of 1935 the government had authorized the issue of Bank of Canada bills in denominations of $1, $2, $5, $10, $20, $50, $100, $500 and $1,000, and the bank had printed them up to the value of $99,000,000. Here then we see the Bank of Canada printing paper currency of little or no value and issuing it with a money value given to it by parliament. The Bank of Canada thus performs with paper currency the same function that the mint performs with metal; it creates Canadian legal tender money. There are very great differences in -the results which occur when the government uses the mint, as a branch of the Department of Finance, to create money, and when the government delegates to the Bank of Canada its power to issue paper currency. One difference is that in the case of the mint all profit on the minting and issuing of metal coins goes to the government, while in the case of the Bank of Canada the profit on the printing and issuing of paper currency is shared between the government and private shareholders who have invested some $5,000,000 in the bank. I would point out that no group of shareholders offering $5,000,000 to an institution that can make money offers any contribution either to the business or
to the power of that bank. What does a bank, which has power to issue $99,000,000, and has issued $99,000,000, receive from a group of shareholders who have invested $5,000,0000 in shares? But that is not the worst part of it. I know that every man who takes the position which I am taking must perforce run counter to public opinion and must be prepared to stand in the condemnation of those who will adhere to the traditions and conventions of the past, not only long after they have been proven to be useless but long after they have been proven to be disastrous to the well-being and the progress of humanity. I am aware that wher men talk of such legislation as we are dealing with to-day they say that it is dictated by the need of security and by the necessities of sound finance. But in my opinion the time is not far distant when laws that give away to a private monopoly the power to create money, laws whereby parliament shares, with men who invest for private profit, its sacred and conspicuous duty of providing the people with an adequate volume of sound and uniform currency, will be looked upon not only as improvident but as thoroughly unsound and bad in constitutional procedure.

creature of law. There can be no money by any rule of nature. There can be money when people rise to the point that their intelligence will permit them to create laws by custom, or there may be such a thing as money when peoples rise to a standard of civilization where they can convene in parliaments for the purpose of enacting laws whereby collectively they can do for the people that which the people cannot do for themselves. My hon. friend should always keep in mind that money is only a simple tool of trade, created primarily to serve as a medium of exchange, created first by a law of custom to assist and advance commerce dependent upon barter, and now developed as the economic bloodstream of a civilization that is living for the firet time when illiteracy has been eliminated and accountancy has come to be generally understood. That is why we have been able to abandon a money of fixed value based upon metal for a token currency whose value comes from law. That is why we are able to take a token currency in the form of paper money and print it upon a basis of twenty-five per cent, and vest in the government the power to withdraw that circulation-

subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS

subtopic: MAJORITY CONTROL BY GOVERNMENT OF CAPITAL STOCK AND BOARD OF DIRECTORS

What I want to point out is this, that if there is one thing upon which this house could have spent a lot of time, and spent it to great advantage, not only to the house but to the whole of the people of Canada, it is that of finding some method to get our medium of exchange effectively into circulation. I venture to say that I have given this subject enough time and study to command the respect of some members of the House of Commons. I have not come to this house without having spent as much time as I could possibly give in the last five years to the study, not only of this particular legislation, but of the monetary system now in vogue throughout the world, the changes that have taken place in the management and control of money, the creation of currency and the credit medium of exchange during many hundred years. This is where I think parliament is making a great and fundamental mistake. We see parliament delegating to the Bank of Canada the identical power to create and issue money that the Department of Finance exercises through the mint. The difference is this, that in the case of the mint the profit from minting money goes to the government, and in the case of Bank of Canada bills it goes to others.

Bank oj Canada

I have dealt with the way in which we create minted coins. I have dealt with the way in which we create Bank of Canada full legal tender money. That is not all the money created by parliament. Let me deal with section 60 of the Bank Act of 1934. Under that section parliament gives away the right to print as money bank note currency. To get a proper appreciation of what that section means the committee shoidd understand that under our Companies Act a limited liability company is incorporated; it has, we shall say, a capital of $1,000,000. That capital is sold; when the capital is paid for, the money is in the treasury; that is the working capital of the company and the shareholders are liable to lose that much money. When you incorporate a bank for a million dollars, however, sell your stock and have a million dollars in the treasury, section 60 of the Bank Act gives the bank the power to print another million dollars in money, and there is no further security required. The only thing the Bank Act says is that where that power to double the capital is enjoyed the liability of the shareholders shall be in the same amount, which is not an additional security but merely an equitable and proper extension of the principle of limited liability which is involved in the Companies Act.
That is what we do when we give our banks the power to print paper money. They can and do buy government bonds with that money. They can and do advance bank loans with that money. They have created an amount of money as great as $140,000,000, and I think it is now somewhere in the vicinity of $118,000,000. I am not unmindful of the fact that under the Bank of Canada Act for five years that amount is to be reduced by five per cent and for another five years by ten per cent until the amount of bank note currency which the banks can issue is reduced to twenty-five per cent. On their present capital they will still be able to issue, free, $36,000,000 of money. Let me recapitulate those figures. There has been in the last year a drop of about $6,000,000 in the amount of silver, nickel and bronze coins, and another substantial drop in the total amount of money in issue. Thus we see that the Department of Finance, representing parliament, issues only $33,000,000 of the total of $252,000,000, in round figures, of token currency in circulation. Parliament creates thirteen per cent of the money and issues it for public use and in terms of public need, while giving away to bankers, who will issue not in terms of public need but only in terms of private gain, the right to issue eighty-seven per cent of the money now in use.
I ask the members of this committee to ponder the situation. In this dominion we have $252,000,000 of money; yet if we look up the records we find that our bank deposits total $2,400,000,000. We do not use either small change currency or large notes as the medium of exchange that carries on the business of this country to-day. The thing that has come to be the medium of exchange is a cheque transferring bank credit, which amounts to ten times the total money in issue in the dominion. I am aware of the fact that certain Canadian bankers have denied that they create money. It is true that they do not create money, but they do monetize credit and use it as a substitute for money, with a bookkeeping system. This is what a banker does when he wants a credit in a bank book, in order to finance a loan, in substitution for the old practice of taking his own capital or the capital that was left on deposit with him and appropriating it from himself or his depositors to a borrower; for that the banker substitutes the writing of a credit into a book, and in that way he just as effectively creates a medium of exchange as does the government when it mints silver coins, or as does the Bank of Canada when it prints bills, or as does a chartered bank when it prints bank note currency.
Let me show you how this works out. As I say, we had $39,000,000 of metal coins in 1934 and only $33,000,000 in 1935, but in Bank of Canada bills, bank notes and bank deposits we have $2,500,000,000. Thus we see that parliament creates only $33,000,000 out of a total of $2,600,000,000 of medium of exchange in common- use, or 33/2600, which is just a little more than one per cent of our money in issue. It is true that those in industry and commerce through individual and collective effort can create wealth up to a point, but they cannot create the money which is necessary to permit a collective enterprise to be carried on in either the production or the distribution of wealth in

human service. When we give away to a banking monopoly that is not responsible to parliament and to the government of the day the power to create money; when we set up in private hands, as we have done, our own Bank of Canada; when we give the chartered banks the power to create paper currency and statements of account which, when transferred by cheque, effectively serve as money, we place the issue of money in the control of those who will not put it into circulation other than under a contract which guarantess its return with interest. Consequently, instead of issuing currency out of the power of government, to advance a general program of progress and the well-being of the community, we find ourselves bogged down under a load of national debts, provincial debts, municipal debts, corporation debts and private debts, that there is nothing available with which to pay.
So what are we going to do? The taxpayers groan under the confiscation of their real estate, and often throw it back on the hands of the municipalities. Men flee from industry because they say that the risk is too great and the taxes are too high. Men actually leave one section of the country to go to another; they are leaving some of our overtaxed cities to-day and are actually leaving our country rather than submit to the confiscation of wealth by taxation which is still increasing. We have done some extraordinary things in this parliament. We have put on an eight per cent sales tax, the highest ever imposed in the Dominion of Canada, and in addition we have proposed to invite the nine provinces to levy additional sales taxes. Well, I speak with some little experience as a municipal administrator, and I say that you can do to investment in business in this country what has already been done to investment in real estate in Canada. You can destroy it by taxation.
This Bank of Canada does not provide, as I thought we promised, a properly constituted central bank which would issue currency and credit in terms of public need, not in terms of private gain. We are not doing that at all; we are perpetuating the worst kind of system, under which the sort of thing I have indicated is carried on, and I just want to draw the attention of hon. members to what it has cost this nation to carry on a system of that kind. These figures should make every hon. member think seriously before he votes for a system to continue the issue of currency and credit in terms of private gain. At the close of the war our national debt stood at $1,400,000,000. Since then we have paid out from consolidated revenue fund 12739-223J
$2,200,000,000 on account of interest. We have paid on account of principal $275,000,000, or, since 1918 a debt cost of $2,475,000,000. Notwithstanding that enormous contribution our national debt in the same period of time has risen from $1,400,000,000 to $3,200,000,000. Taking the average of our deficits and interest charges as we now face them in 1936, averaging them back to 1931, we are going behind at the rate of S2.400,000.000 a decade. And that is only the federal account. The municipal account is just as bad; the provincial account is just as bad, and the load of corporation and personal debt is bringing disaster everywhere.
What has parliament done in the past? Influenced and directed by those who claim a special knowledge of political economy and monetary control, it has said that parliament cannot be trusted with the issue of money; that it would spend too much, and that, therefore, we must put the brakes on by borrowing at interest and have the taxpayer stand behind to defy governments and put them out if they dare to spend too much.
But that did not work. Parliament said: Let us throw the burden on posterity. We borrowed to build roads, to build railways, and to build bridges across the St. Lawrence, believing that posterity was to carry the load. But, unfortunately for this generation, we have caught up to posterity, and the load which we thought posterity was going to bear we find that we cannot carry ourselves. A debt system is not a sound money system. A debt claim system, under which men interested in interest bearing bonds control the issue of currency and credit, is not a safe system. If we are going to have progress financed and democracy maintained we must do what has been done with the post office, administer it as a public utility largely free from partisan influence. We must do with our money system what we have done with out customs' system, administer it as a public undertaking largely free from partisan influence, and build it up until it earns the respect of everyone. We must establish the Bank of Canada as the supreme court of finance in the dominion and have men in charge of it who will serve just as honestly and efficiently and effectively as the men in the supreme court of Canada. That is not an impossible proposal. The Minister of Finance will agree that t'he Commonwealth Bank of Australia has no capital stock at all, and this kind of institution should not have any stock.

For some time, Mr. Chairman, I have been worried over the price of Canadian bacon in Great Britain. I have before me quotations showing that Danish bacon brings two cents a pound more in Great Britain than does our Canadian bacon, and those who will take the trouble to look up prices will find that the Danish farmer receives 4-7 cents a pound more for his bacon than we do in Canada. There are complaints that the bales in which bacon is shipped out of this country are not put up uniformly; that a poor piece of bacon will be put with a good piece, and for many years the type of bacon going out of Canada has not been regulated. There are five grades of No. 1 Canadian bacon, and we think the grading of bacon that is shipped out of Canada would help a great deal in this situation. We also feel that if our bacon wore of a uniform quality, this would help a great deal. I should be glad if the minister would tell us how many different grades of bacon there are in No. 1 that is shipped out of this country.
There is another angle to the question. Those who are best informed on the matter tell us that we have not the right type of bacon hog. We have reports from a friend of the minister, Mr. Schneider in Kitchener, and from Mr. J. S. McLean, of Canada Packers that it would mean twelve millions of dollars to Canada if we got a different type of pig, say the Danish pig. The Danes have specialized in bacon and dairying for the last seventy years, and have surpassed other nations in that field. The Danish pigs have proven themselves to be the best breeding stock. While the trade agreement helped to a certain extent, the fact remains that the Danes are pushing us right off the British market and getting a better price for their bacon. One of the reasons why we want the Danish pig in Canada is that at birth they are twice the size of the Yorkshire pig. They are much better mothers and have smaller shoulders and necks. They have larger hams which will grow faster and will weigh 225 pounds four weeks earlier than the Yorkshire pig. The Danish pig is wanted by the Canadian packer. This may not be inter-

esting to some of the Toronto members, but it is interesting to the farmers who live north of Toronto, and it certainly is interesting to the people in my district. These people have been driven to extreme need, and it must not 'be forgotten that it is generally the pigs that pay the mortgage on the farm. Mr. J. S. McLean, President of Canada Packers Limited, 'has stated that if Canadian hogs had been as good as Danish hogs, during the last three years the Canadian farmer would have received $12,000,000 more for his hogs. That is a great deal of money, and I think attention should be directed to this statement.
For eight years I have tried to get the Danish hog into Canada, but there is an oligarchy in the Department of Agriculture past which it was impossible to get. There is a man in the department who occupies a room nearly as large as this chamber. Things have gone to his head and he believes he- is Mussolini. I think it is time that the officials of this department should be told what they should do. Our ministers have had great difficulty. The hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell), when he was minister, tried to get the Danish pig into Canada, but he was not successful. The former Minister of Agriculture, Mr. Weir, tried to get them in. The department agreed to let in the landrace pig from Sweden, but they would not let in the Danish pig. The Swedish pig is much inferior, but the former minister had to abide by the ruling of the oligarchy. The present Minister (Mr. Gardiner) has told me, both publicly and privately, that he will help me to get the Danish pig in. I know he has his battles to fight and I know those in the animal husbandry division will try hard to see that he does not get the Danish pig in. Nevertheless he has given his promise and I rely on it. This would mean many millions of dollars to the people of Canada. I think this matter comes under the Department of Trade and Commerce as it really means trying to get as much as we can for the production of our farmers.

Mr. Chairman, I want to draw just one matter to the attention of the minister. At one time we enjoyed a promising trade in pure bred cattle with New Zealand and Australia, but this trade has been lost. At the present time most of it is going to the United States. I take some farm papers and I am well aware of the fact that the United States are very proud that they have been able to get the representatives of the governments of Australia and New Zealand to purchase suitable pure bred stock in that country. We have trade commissioners in New Zealand

and Australia, and I think they should be notified that there is in Canada pure bred stock which will compare very favourably with anything there is in the United States. When the governments of those two countries again send their representatives abroad to secure pure bred stock, our trade commissioners should invite them to come to this country. It might be -asked if this stock can be obtained in Canada. I may say that within the last three weeks I have had the opportunity of visiting some herds in Ontario and I say most definitely and emphatically that we have some wonderful pure bred cattle. I am a practical man and I know what I am talking about. I have reared stock which was good enough to go to Australia and New Zealand. I urge the minister to take up this matter with the trade commissioners who should ask the representatives of the governments of these countries at least to visit Canada to see what they can get from their sister dominion.
