There is a matter which I think should receive the minister's attention. The hon. member for Wellington North (Mr. Blair) very properly raised the question of the sides from the number of grades of hogs that are included in what is known as grade A export bacon, but I did not notice that the minister referred to that question at all.

Because it does not come
under this department.

In a way, yes. Probably
it comes under no department, but certainly it should come under the Department of Trade and Commerce in conjunction with the Department of Agriculture. I know that the Department of Agriculture undertakes to handle all the grading of live stock and all that sort of thing so far as Canada is concerned, and when any action is necessary in connection with the export of live stock or the grading of live stock products the Department of Agriculture is usually consulted and I believe its views and expert advice largely dominate. But if any action is taken it must be taken through the Department of Trade and Commerce, that is, action definitely fixing the grade of export products. Now this is what was found in the investigation by the price spreads commission. I will read a part of the evidence which bears out what my hon. friend from Wellington North had to say on the subject. I shall quote two or three paragraphs because I think it
is desirable that this matter should be taken into consideration and some definite policy adopted. I quote from page 171 of the report of the commission:
Summing up, we feel that the system at present in vogue in handling Canadian bacon on the British market operates primarily to the advantage of the packer exporter and the distributor concerns on the British market, and that there is insufficient consideration given to the interest of the primary producer. If, however, as the president of Canada Packers has declared, the price of bacon in Great Britain fixes the price of hogs in Canada, it is obviously of vital importance to the producer of hogs that the marketing of Canadian bacon should be on a fair and equitable basis.
Evidence given us has shown that it was possible to secure for high class Canadian bacon a price substantially in advance of the prevailing price and a figure practically equivalent to that of Danish bacon.
I pause here to emphasize this particular point. The minister a moment ago referred to the firm of Schneiders, though he modestly refrained from mentioning the name, inasmuch as the firm happens to be in his own riding. There is another firm, Dumarts, which has just as good a record, but it was Schneiders' bacon with which an interesting test was made in London. One of those who carried out the test was a gentleman named Percival, I believe, though I am not sure of this, one of the most prominent in the marketing of bacon in London, and with him were Miss Cora Hinds of the Winnipeg Free Press and a third person. They were to be the judges. They took bacon from some of Schneiders' export, and they also took Danish, Irish and Dutch bacon, all leading brands. These samples they took to an expert chef in one of the outstanding hotels and after he had cooked the bacon and served it in the ordinary way this committee, without knowing where any particular sample came from, passed upon the best type, and they all agreed on a certain selection which proved to be Schneiders' bacon.
Another evidence that we can do as well or nearly as well as the Danish producers is [DOT]the experience of the Ontario Department of Agriculture with what is known as the Big "0" Brand. In this connection I wish to commend the present provincial Minister of Agriculture, Mr. Duncan Marshall, for having carried on that experiment-because it was largely an experiment. The abattoir that produced that brand, with the assistance of the Ontario government, took select bacon hogs for the purpose of making export bacon. I shall come to the significance of that in a moment, but for the purpose of this recital it is sufficient to refer to that in passing. They then exported their bacon to a committee of British distributors among whom,

I believe, are two agents of Canada Packers, that is, British firms who are agents of Canada Packers in Great Britain, and other distributors. They constitute a marketing committee in England, and every Thursday they sit and determine what is to be the price of bacon for the following week. In other words, the price of Canadian bacon is fixed by a committee of British distributors of bacon, not only Canadian but other bacon as well. The Big "O" Brand was exported independently of that committee and one outstanding firm-I will not mention the name because they have been penalized and forced to abandon the handling of that brand-secured a price which equalled the Danish price in several instances, exceeded it in one or two instances, and in other instances was slightly below, a mere shilling or two below, whereas the prevailing rate for Canadian bacon was eight, ten, and sometimes fourteen shillings below the Danish. As a rule it is substantially below the rate for Danish bacon. I do not have the record, though, under my hand. But the Big "O" Brand, shipment after shipment, secured that market on a parity, either slightly above or slightly below the Danish price. It is safe to say that it was virtually on a parity with the Danish price. This committee to which I have referred served notice on the British firm that was distributing the Big "0" Brand- I have seen the letters, but here again one cannot use these things because it only penalizes people-directing them to desist and come into the committee again. And they did. I have no means of ascertaining how the Big "0" Brand has been marketed during the past year. That is not within my knowledge and I cannot therefore deal with it. Now, why is it that Canadian bacon has received a lower price on the British market than Danish bacon? I can give the answer by quoting further from the report dealing with the evidence before the price spreads commission. I shall repeat a part of what I have already read:
Evidence given us has shown that it was possible to secure for high-class Canadian bacon a price substantially in advance of the prevailing price and a figure practically equivalent to that of Danish bacon. This, however, was secured only through British marketing agencies other than those included in the British Bacon Committee. It was also pointed out that predatory action had been taken by the bacon committee to discourage independent dealers from handling Canadian bacon, such as the Big '0' Brand at a price obove the "official" price.
These are the facts. There is no question about them. I want the minister to follow this very carefully:

The packing companies include in grade A, bacon made from several classes of hogs, including selects, butcher, light, heavies-
And bacon. That is, five grades of hogs included in the production of what is known as grade A bacon. Your bacon hog fixes the price of hogs in Canada. Selects get $1 per hundred above the bacon price.
A dollar per hog.

A dollar per hog above
the bacon price. The lights are penalized a dollar a hog; the heavies are penalized one and a half to two dollars a hog, and the butchers are penalized a dollar a hog in the market. Mr. McLean swore very positively- I have his evidence before me-that the price of all Canadian hogs was fixed by the price of bacon on the British market. The best price for Canadian hogs is for what is known as the bacon grade. He, however, who exports about eighty to ninety per cent of the bacon, included in the class of bacon that fixes the price in England five grades of hogs, including those three lower grades. It must be evident to anyone that the inclusion of those three lower grades in their grade A bacon, which determined the price of bacon in England, reacted adversely upon the price of hogs in Canada. One cannot escape that conclusion,
I turn now to a fact affecting interdepartmental officials. When I occupied the office which is now held by the minister, this question of the export of Canadian bacon was before me, and I may say to the minister that he has in Mr. Wilson an expert excellently versed- in the marketing of farm products. Through Mr. Wilson and other sources we learn that the type of Canadian, bacon which was going forward to Great Britain was inferior, and that if we were to raise the price of bacon on the British market we should have to improve the export standard. So I asked for a conference, and a conference was held between officials of the Department of Agriculture and the minister of that department, and officials of the Trade and Commerce department and myself. Present at that conference were two representatives of Canada- Packers. One was Mr. Todd, who claims to be the representative of the packers, but who, as everyone is aware who knows his connections, represents Mr. McLean, and the other was a gentleman who is not with that company but who at that time was its sales manager. At that conference it was demonstrated, from advices we had in the department, that it was the inferior type of bacon going forward which was responsible for the low price we were

receiving on the British market as contrasted with Danish bacon. My effort was to interest the Department of Agriculture in raising that standard, which could be done by eliminating the use in grade A of the three inferior grades of hogs and limiting it to bacon and select hogs. But at that conference the officials of the Department of Agriculture turned to Mr. Todd, and' he it was who determined what the policy would be. His answer was along this line. He said, "There is a market in England for second bacon, and it is our opinion that it is better to export a substantial quantity of what might be determined second bacon, because there is a market for it." My argument was-and I believe that any expert in the Department of Trade andi Commerce will endorse it- that if we were to raise the standard of our export bacon by including a larger proportion of select and bacon hogs in grade A or by limiting grade A to those two selections, we should raise the price of bacon in England and automatically raise the price of hogs in Canada, because, as Mr. McLean said, the price of hogs in Canada was fixed by the price of bacon in England. Do not let us forget that we export only about fifteen per cent and we consume in Canada eighty-five per cent. So that the price of hogs marketed in Canada as well as of those exported to Great Britain is fixed by British prices for our bacon.
It may and probably will be argued that there is not a sufficient quantity of select and bacon hogs in Canada to make this suggestion practicable. The evidence showed that about twenty per oent were selects and thirty per cent were bacon; in other words, about fifty per cent of the hogs marketed wild grade bacon or select. So, as the total export is only about fifteen per cent, there is in Canada an abundant supply of high grade hogs to serve the market in Great Britain, the market we should most earnestly foster and develop, and yet to leave an adequate supply in this country for high class trade at home. But let us assume that the argument has some foundation, that there is not enough to supply our whole export requirements and attend to the demand in Canada. Then I submit-and this is what I rose to suggest to the minister-that there should be a definite regulation to limit the class of hogs used for the production of grade A bacon to selects and bacons; the others can go, if it is desired, into grade B bacon. But it is grade A bacon that fixes the price for Canada on the markets of Great Britain.
Let me read further from the report. After describing the types of hogs that go into the
production of grade A bacon, the report continues :
That the bacon committee in Great Britain is composed of British distributors who work m close collaboration with the Canadian packers, discloses, in our opinion, a condition m the marketing of Canadian bacon in Great Britain which demands the attention of an independent body with government authority in order that the producers' interests may be properly protected.
I think that is extremely important. They go on to say:
We recommend that a board be set up to supervise the live stock and meat production industry. This board should, in our opinion-
I would say here, this board or some other body:
immediately on its appointment make a earetul survey of the situation in the British market with a view to:
(a)	Ascertaining to what extent Canadian packers and the British bacon committee operate as a mutual body; and
(b)	To revise the grading of export bacon so as to ensure the highest possible price for Canadian selects and bacon hogs; and
(c)	To secure such a system of distribution as will satisfactorily meet the requirements of the British trade, while at the same time ensuring full and adequate protection to the producer of hogs in Canada.
As far as I know that has not been done. I am bringing it to the attention of the minister and of his colleague the Minister of Agriculture. I urge them to examine the reporl of the price spreads commission in this regard and to make a searching investigation of these facts, because the whole hog industry of Canada, that is the interests of the primary producers, is definitely adversely affected by the present method of marketing bacon in England. I had not any idea that this question would come up to-night, and'I have not in my hand certain statistics, I will, however, quote from memory, and I am pretty sure that my memory will not be much astray. I believe the facts I am about to give will surprise the committee.
After this report was made I carried on some further investigations of my own to satisfy myself on this point because I believe that the price of hogs-and incidentally the price of cattle, though we are talking about bacon and hogs just now-is of tremendous importance not only to the farmer but also to the economic structure of Canada. I will tell the committee why I say so. One thing that is evident above everything else in our discussions of the monetary question, unemployment and so on is that there is a shortage of purchasing power in the country, particularly among the farmers. Inasmuch as the farming community constitutes nearly fifty per cent of our population it follows as day

follows night that if you can raise the prices of their products you increase the purchasing power of the farmers. In raising the prices of hogs we would be making one of the major, underlying, fundamental contributions towards recovery in this dominion.

Would the hon. gentleman permit a question? I gather from his remarks that he thinks it would be necessary to import Danish hogs in order to produce English breakfast bacon in Canada. Is that my hon. friend's idea?
I was not talking about that.
The hon. gentleman mentioned hogs being shipped in from Denmark.

I am entirely in favour of importing pure bred stock from either Denmark or Sweden, both of which are excellent types. I am entirely in favour of that being done in order to improve the stock in Canada, but I am trying to emphasize this: With the stock we have, without waiting for the improvement of the stock by the processes suggested, we can make a substantial contribution to the correction of this situation.
This is what I found, to which I was about to refer: I took Mr. McLean's statement that the price of Canadian hogs was fixed according to the price of bacon in the British market. Of course he went on to say that there were certain costs, spreads and so on which helped to determine the price, but the point was that it was the price we received on the British market which fixed the price of our hogs. Taking that as a basis I made an investigation; I said to myself: Well, if that applies to Canada it must apply also to Denmark and Holland, two of our chief competitors, and to other countries. I was able to get comparative figures from Denmark and Holland, and this is what I found: I have long sheets of these figures covering a period of two years, and the Danish farmer was receiving for his hogs about six,- seven or eight cents a pound more than the Canadian farmer was receiving, using the same ratio in each case. The Dutch farmer received from three cents to five or six cents a pound more. The average for two years showed that these farmers received about 4J cents per pound more for their hogs than did the Canadian farmer. There would have to be a slight _ deduction made in one case and an addition in another. In the case of Holland, which was the most comparable country with Canada, Holland was on a gold basis and there was the question of freight, but even if we make those allowances, it would vary only slightly the figure I gave a moment ago.

What I am coming to is this: Here in Canada we accept from the packers a dictum, if you like, a definite determining factor that fixes the price of hogs. It is not the government; it has nothing to do with the government. It is not parliament; parliament has nothing to do with it. The bare fact is that the price of bacon in England is so and so and the price of hogs in Canada will bear a certain relation to that price. Even accepting it on that basis we have a right to demand that the Canadian farmer should receive as fair a proportion of that British pound or dollar, as the case may be, as does the Dutch or Danish farmer, and that is not the case to-day.
I have gone into this matter in this way to demonstrate that in my opinion-and I have worked it out with the assistance of some very able statisticians-this runs into enormous sums of money. From memory I hesitate to intimate what the figures are, but they amount to millions and millions of dollars a year that I firmly believe the Canadian farmers at least are being deprived of, if not defrauded of, by the practice in force at the present time. In this report we have the finding, which as I recall it was fairly unanimous if not entirely so, that the government or some authority created by parliament should go into this whole question for the purpose of seeing that the Canadian farmer gets a fair price for his hogs. He is not receiving that fair price to-day. It is easy for statisticians representing the packers to say there is so much cost for this, so much for that and so much for the other thing, and then show a fraction of a cent a pound profit spread over all their operations. That is quite simple, but it is not the whole story. We have all the facts and figures in the report. Every table of statistics submitted shows that prices of farm products have dropped lower than those of any other major schedule. During the past six years, when the farmer has been subjected to the most difficult times of his history, the packers made more money than they ever did before. That is the point. Oh, I know the answer to that, that if you took all those profits and divided them among the millions of farmers, what would it amount to? That is not the point. On reflection we must always remember that when Canada Packers were organized in their present form they gathered in a number of independent packing concerns of which I think six were closed down, representing an investment of some millions of dollars. All that overhead is now taken out of the price of processing the hogs, but that plant is not operating.

*Some of those great plants, which cost millions of dollars, such as the plant at Ingersoll, a portion of the Davis plant, and others of that kind, are used merely as storage yards. But the entire capital cost of the plants that were closed down remains in the capital structure, and the plants operating at present must provide through their processing charge the overhead for the whole structure.
In addition to that, the record shows that Canada Packers have created a reserve which in another five years will completely wipe out all the old investment, including that in the closed plants as well as the investment in the operating plants, as well as paying back dividends for some years, and of course they have also paid very handsome dividends and bonuses all through this period. Now I am not attacking a concern for being successful, but when that concern is so fabulously successful as it has been in the past five or six years during a time when the farmers suffered more than at any other time, that fact is worthy of consideration.
In the second place I say that they and they alone fix the price of hogs. No government body does it; the Department of Agriculture, the Department of Trade and Commerce, the provincial governments, the dominion government none of them has a word to say, but at ten o'clock every morning the price is fixed, fixed by virtually the one man, and fixed, as he says, on the basis of the price of bacon in England.

Is it really a fact that it is
fixed on that basis?

Yes, he swears to it. I
have it before me somewhere. This is not the exact item I was going to quote, but this refers to it:
Mr. McLean: You see if the British market advances the Canadian price here goes up immediately, and if the market declines, the Canadian price goes down immediately; and the hogs are bought on the basis of the English market practically all the time. Kemember that is not an absolute rule, because there are a hundred variations to it. But the variation from the export basis is always small.
There is another quotation, which for the moment I cannot put my finger on, in which he makes it even more definite than that. However, I think that will serve the purpose for the moment.
Therefore I say in the second place, the price of hogs being fixed on the basis of the price of bacon in England is a very serious matter, but the most serious of all is the British bacon committee. That committee sits once a week and determines what the price of Canadian bacon on the British market shall

be. There is no open market for Canadian bacon in Great Britain. Lest I should be misunderstood let me say at once that I do not wish to disparage the value of the British market to Canada; it is of tremendous importance, and we ought to cooperate with the British distributor in every possible way. I am not suggesting that we should do anything foolish or reckless, but I say that we have a right, in the interests of the producers of hogs in this country, whose price is subject to fixation in England, to have something to say on the fixing of that price. At the present time we have nothing to say. As is recommended in the report, the whole question should be carefully examined into. This should not be done in any reckless way; it should be done with great care. I understand that the minister is going over to England this year, and I think it is wise that he should. I suggest to him that while he is there he should look into this whole matter. He should not place himself wholly in the hands of the bacon committee; that might be more disastrous still. But if he goes over there suitably informed on the whole subject I believe that he will be able, with his well known sound common sense to see through the whole business.
I deprecate vigorously the restrictions that have been placed against independent exporters. I believe that there has been some improvement in that respect in the last year, but I am convinced that there is not the freedom of marketing which there ought to be. I believe that we should encourage exporters such as Schneider, Dumarts, and other smaller exporters, many of whom have established a reputation which we can well be proud of and whose bacon is equal to the best foreign bacon on that market.
Do they come under the control of that committee?
Speaking as to the past, I believe they were absolutely under its control. That statement may have to be modified as far as last year is concerned; I cannot speak as to that.

Before this item carries I wish to raise what may be a point of order, but perhaps I might bring it within the ambit of the item under consideration by asking the Minister of Trade and Commerce how we come to be on estimates this evening in defiance of the announced program last Friday night. This is the program as announced:
Mr. Bennett: What business will be taken up on Monday?
Mr. Mackenzie (Vancouver)-
Who apparently was leading the house for the government-
-We are prepared to proceed with any of the bills on the order paper.
It is a well known rule, although I cannot point to any paragraph in Beauchesne or Bourinot, but a rule sanctioned by perhaps forty years of usage in this house, that the last thing at night the leader of the opposition asks what is to be the program for the next day, and is advised by the minister who is leading the house. A habit had grown up to some extent-it was worse in the last house and it is worse in this-of departing from that procedure and taking up any item which happens to be convenient. This is not the first or second or third time this session that either estimates have been taken up when none was foretold, or certain estimates have been taken up that were not mentioned. It is absolutely essential that there be some faith in these matters. It is impossible for 245 men to be in the house all the time; they must go and attend to their letters and other business; a half empty house often does more efficient work, because the men are there who are interested in the subject, and if we are all to sit here all the time this will make for a great deal of delay. The hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens), in the midst of his very able remarks a few minutes ago, said that he had not the slightest idea that this was coming up to-night or he would have had his data ready. Are we all to sit here without the slightest idea whether an item is coming up, and bring our notes morning,

noon and night in case it should? Does that make for cooperation? The government may say: Oh, well, we are going to do it and what are you going to do about it? But not a day passes without some member of the government having to ask the consent of the house- and that means unanimous consent-to pass a bill through some stage. The Minister of Finance did this on Friday night. Any one man can block it. I am not suggesting that as a threat or a hold-up or a filibuster, for I want to go home. But this is an illustration of the truth that we need cooperation; cooperation can be founded only upon good faith, and good faith I take to mean that when it is announced that the program will be so and so the announcement should be adhered to. I would suggest that whoever is leading the house for the government make a note of that, and that when a statement is made it be adhered to. If we are going to take estimates, say so; and if we are going to take estimates, indicate which estimates, and then adhere to that program.

I was not in the house the other night when the announcement was made, but perhaps I should take any responsibility for what may appear to my hon. friend as a breach of faith. Certainly there is no intention whatsoever of taking any advantage of the committee in bringing up these estimates to-night. The explanation, as a matter of fact, is very, very simple indeed. It may be known to my hon. friend that there is some intention on the part of some of us to proceed abroad during the summer; as it happens, one of the officials of the Department of Trade and Commerce intends to proceed to Great Britain in the course of a very few days, and it was thought desirable, before he leaves, to take the estimates of the branch with which he is particularly concerned. That is the simple explanation. I would also say that if the committee feel that any advantage is being taken of hon. members and they prefer that we rise and report progress, I am quite willing to do so, but it never entered my mind that we were taking advantage of anyone in connection with the matter.

I do not wish to delay matters unnecessarily, but the minister has been trying to get his estimates before the committee for some time. They have been announced repeatedly, at least on three former occasions, as coming up, but because of the length of the debate on some other matter it was quite impossible to bring on the estimates on the day arranged. Now it is getting to the time when it becomes almost imperative that something 'be done about the matter, and that is why these estimates were brought up to-night. If, however, the committee think there is any breach of faith, I do not wish to continue with these estimates to-night.
It is the hon. gentlemen who have not come back from Toronto or elsewhere who would probably have more of a grievance.

Possibly, Mr. Chairman, we have overlooked the fact that the Prime Minister said the other evening that we should be prepared to take up any items on the order paper because we had reached that stage of the session. The other evening when the hon. gentleman who was leading the *house said that we would take up any bills on the order paper I thought he had in mind anything on the order paper, as the Prime Minister had said on the previous evening, and this evening when it was mentioned to me that the discussion on the Bank of Canada Act was to be discontinued and Trade and Commerce estimates taken up, I am bound to say that I did not think this strange because when we are within perhaps two weeks or so of the end of the session the government usually says at the adjournment, when asked what will be the business of tomorrow: You must 'be prepared to take up any items on the order paper. I should like to disabuse the mind of the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps) as to there being an embargo on Russian trade. Apparently the reiteration of what took place has no effect on him. The former Liberal administration, it will be recalled, terminated diplomatic relations with Russia, but they did not in any way deal with the trade situation. The late government passed a statute empowering the governor in council to prohibit importations from any country that had not been a party to the treaty of Versailles, having regard to the labour provisions of that treaty, and subsequently there was a prohibition by order in council on the importation into Canada of anthracite coal, pulpwood, certain kinds of furs, and one other item. The reasons were obvious. These goods were being dumped on this market. There is no reason why trade with Russia may not be carried on to-day just as with any other country, or why Russia could not carry on trade with Canada just as any other country trades with Canada, except

with respect to the commodities I have mentioned. The reason for those items being dealt with as they were has been explained so frequently to the committee that I shall not bother restating it.
All I referred to was the embargo on trade. I made no further reference.
There is no embargo.
Then why are we not doing trade with Russia?
We are in certain commodities.

Then there is an embargo on other commodities. I did not say that there was an embargo on everything, but I say that the government, if they so desired, could remove the embargo which now exists. Now that the matter has been brought up again, perhaps the minister would inform the committee against what goods coming from Russia there is an embargo.
If you wish to call it an embargo, it is imposed against timber, asbestos, pulp and dressed furs.
Undressed furs.
Undressed furs come in. There have been serious protests from manufacturers in this country against dressed furs coming in.
Originally it was the whole class of dressed furs. Then there was a modification of it.
Have not the breaking off of diplomatic relations with Russia and the embargo, or call it what you will, had the effect of almost entirely disrupting trade between Canada and Russia?

Perhaps I could answer that by saying that the trade is not so large as it might be if the embargo, if you call it such, were not applied. There is a certain disruption of trade, but I cannot give any figures at the moment.
Has the minister any figures that would show the trade between this country and Russia in the last few years?
No, I have not.

Is there no mention of Prince Rupert or New Westminster?
Not in this.
Do other subsidies refer to other ports?
There may be calls at Prince Rupert in the British Columbia and China servioe.
Just the China service?
But not the New Zealand.
I did not quite catch the minister's explanation of the fifty per cent increase.

The statement was made by the ship owners that the competition from United States lines was becoming severe because of their better boats and also because of the fact that the United States government was subsidizing their vessels very heavily. I 'believe the Matson line is the one interested, and the Canadian company finds it very difficult to operate under these conditions.
Could the minister give us an idea of what subsidies the United States government are paying?
They pay on a speed basis.
The United States subsidies to the Matson line amount to $1,192,080.

To the one line only?

Supply-Trade-Mail Subsidies
To the Matson line.

How many boats do they run 'between United States ports and the
orient?
They run four.

Does the minister differentiate between ships of Canadian and ships of foreign registry in the granting of subsidies? I ask that question because when boats of foreign registry are chartered it is frequently agreed that they shall engage foreign masters and foreign crews, and if something could be done to secure ships of Canadian registry it would benefit Canadian trade and employment.

We do not discriminate with respect to registry. As a matter of fact there are not many vessels registered in Canada. The Canadian Pacific boats are registered in England. As regards the employment of men on boats, the matter was referred to a committee after the last occasion on which the estimates were under consideration, and the committee has not reported.
Has anything definite been arrived at yet as a result of the negotiations that have been going on for a faster service to Australia and New Zealand?
Not yet.

I suggest to the minister that the service between British Columbia Pacific ports and New Zealand and Australia is a very important one to Canada from the standpoint both of maintaining trade and of the mail service, and the subsidy which is paid is quite a modest one compared with the service that is involved. The vessels were excellent ten years ago but they are not now up to date; in fact they are obsolete. There is a good deal of business being lost to the Matson line. It is true that line receives a subsidy of over $1,000,000 and it has faster and more up to date vessels. The result is that Canada is losing business to that line. I have always had in mind that we should negotiate with the Union Steamship Company of New Zealand, of which the Canadian Pacific is now half-owner, for a faster and more efficient service with more modern vessels, even if it is necessary to increase the subsidy. Another factor that should be kept in mind with respect to these larger items is that these lines carry mail. I have figured it out on two or three occasions, and if we paid for the mail at the usual rate, so much per ton or hundredweight, or whatever the rate is, we should have to pay almost as much as

many of these subsidies amount to. Therefore, when we discuss the question of subsidies we must remember that the service covers a very valuable mail service. I would suggest to the minister, now that he has increased the subsidy to $300,000, that a definite effort should be made to put on faster steamships and possibly to give a more frequent service. At any rate there should be faster and more modern ships. I certainly believe that the service is one which it is well worth sustaining. The minister himself referred to the pending negotiation for a revision of the trade treaty with Australia, which by the way has been a very valuable treaty to Canada, resulting in a considerable increase in business, and much in Canada's favour. All these matters ought to be safeguarded. But the question of subsidy should be considered in connection with these other points to which I have referred.

The minister will recall that when we last diisicussed this item we spent some time going into the relative merits of the Matson boats and our own. The Matson boats have a 22 knot sea speed and receive the subsidy based upon speed, plus loans from the government, to enable them to build ships by paying an interest of 1J per cent, in one case. The Royal Mail have indicated in their published statement that they have an interest with the Canadian Pacific in this line that runs from our Pacific coast to Australia and New Zealand, not the Union Steamship Company of New Zealand but the Royal Mail as the second partner. They purchased their interest from the Canadian Pacific for preference shares in the Canadian Pacific, and in their last annual statement they indicated that they had not received interest this last year or two in connection with the shares they thus acquired. I saw the other day that negotiations were pending between the Royal Mail and the Canadian Pacific, and the government of Australia, the government of New Zealand, the government of Canada, and possibly the Fiji Islands, through their appropriate representatives, looking towards a more speedy service that would be more comparable with the 22 knot sea speed service of the Matson line. The minister says that negotiations are still pending and that nothing has yet been definitely concluded, but it is quite obvious that a great deal of our mail which comes from England and which ordinarily would go through Vancouver has been diverted to boats at San Francisco for the purpose of finding speedy transport to Australia. Perhaps the minister will recall that when a former Prime Minister of Australia came to this

Supply-Trade-Mail Subsidies
country last he came to San, Francisco because of difficulties of securing accommodation which would suit his plans at the time and because of the slow rate of speed at which he would travel as compared with the speed of the Matson line boats. If the minister is not in a position to say what negotiations have been carried on, or to what extent they have been proceeded with, I can quite understand his not having a statement to make. I may be wrong, buit is it not the Royal Mail that has the interest to which I have referred?

I was going to correct my right hon. friend. The partnership exists between the Canadian Pacific and the Union Steamship Company of New Zealand. The Union Steamship Company, I am told, is owned by the P. & O.
P. & O. is what I meant to say, and not the Royal Mail. Mr. Shaw is chairman of the board.

All hon. members appreciate, and certainly the members of the government appreciate the extreme value of the service to Australia and New Zealand, largely because of the trade with those countries, which is very much in our favour. The boats which are now in the service, as the leader of the opposition says, are slower and more or less obsolete, and to my knowledge that is a matter of special concern to the owners. I cannot say anything more at the moment than that the situation is, to put it mildly, being explored thoroughly with the idea of putting on a better service. That is the position in which the matter stands now and I cannot give any other definite information at the moment.
We have only two, sometimes three boats, and the Matson line has four.

It is not necessary to remind the minister, because he is familiar with the fact, that we have a Pacific port which is served by the Canadian National Railways, the port of Prince Rupert. That port is equal to any on the Pacific coast, and when the question of subsidies is under consideration by this or any future government I think we should at least give some consideration to a port that is served by the nationally owned railway, a port that has facilities to carry Canadian trade and to bring back the products of other countries. I have no criticism to offer with regard to subsidies, but I would impress upon the minister that when the question is under consideration Vancouver and Victoria are not the only ports which should receive attention, because we have
another port which, as I say, is served by the nationally owned railway. Moreover, behind that railway system we have hinterland which statesmen in past years have regarded as valuable enough to warrant development, and it is up to the statesmen of to-day and of the future to find out whether that opinion is really sound and, if it is, to do something to assist in the development of that hinterland in British Columbia. I ask the minister to make a special note of that and to realize that we have on the Pacific British North American coast a port which is served by a nationally owned railway.

I wish to congratulate my
hon. friend upon the case he puts up for his good port of Prince Rupert. As he knows, we are not prone to make promises, except this, that we shall certainly give every consideration to his representations when the time comes.

I observe that the minister
has cut off half the subsidy on the steamships between this country and Great Britain. Is that going to affect in any way the services between Canada and Great Britain?

No; it will not affect them at all. I think I gave the explanation before. The cut has been made because the statement of the companies showed that they had done substantially better last year than they did the year before. In fact, if my memory serves me aright, prior to 1930 they were not receiving any subsidy at all.
I notice there are nine items on the Pacific ocean. Might I ask if they all include the free carriage of mail on the routes indicated?

I cannot give the number
of them, but in some of them the Post Office Department contributes towards the subsidy.
Which ones?
The Post Office Department contributes to these services: Vancouver and northern ports of British Columbia; Victoria, Vancouver, way ports and Skagway; and Victoria and west coast Vancouver island.
Is that all?
That is all.

They draw a subsidy under
this item, a mail subsidy it is called, and then the post office pays as well for the carrying of mail. Is that not a unique situation?
The post office assists.

And so they draw two subsidies. One is a mail subsidy, and they are

Supply-Trade-Mail Subsidies
paid for carrying the mail as well. Does the minister not think it should be either one or the other? If they get a mail subsidy for carrying the mail they should carry the mail, should they not? Or if they do not get the mail subsidy they are paid for carrying it according to weight and measurement. But apparently in these cases they get both subsidies. What is the explanation?

Nearly all subsidies are given not only for carrying the mail. That is merely a portion of the service which is rendered. We may say that, of a subsidy of S200,000 given a certain steamship company, $100,000 or $150,000 might fairly be for the carriage of the mails; the balance of it would be for the encouragement of the service itself, not necessarily having anything to do with the carriage of the mails. But in nearly all cases the total amount of the subsidy includes the cost of carrying the mails; over and beyond that it is for the service.

I suppose the minister, not
being connected with the department, would not have the amounts paid by the post office?
The Post Office Department would have to give that information.
What is the total amount of the subsidy granted to the Union Steamship Company, Vancouver?
Eighteen thousand dollars.

I have a question to ask the minister. I notice that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company in their annual report have incorporated both their steamships and their railways. They aire two separate corporations. One is Canadian Pacific Ocean Steamships Limited and the other is the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. It is impossible from their report to tell whether they are making their profits out of the railways or out of the steamships. Under steamship depreciation, in their Canadian Pacific Railway Company report to their shareholders, they have taken out of their profit and loss account $3,550,996 for depreciation, and I also find that they have lumped the number of ships which they have both on the Atlantic and on the Pacific. They start with their five freight boats of 10,000 tons dead weight capacity, called the Beaver boats: then they come to the Duchess boats; then they come to the Empress of Asia, the Empress of Australia, the Empress of Britain, the Empress of Canada, the Empress of Japan and the Empress of Russia; then they come to the Mont boats, the Montclair, the Montcalm and the Montrose. Some of these ships are

operated on the Pacific. Five of them, freight ships, are operated from London, and the Duchess boats and the Mont boats are operated from Liverpool as passenger and freight boats. I should like to know whether the subsidy paid to the Canadian Pacific is paid to the Canadian Pacific Railway for their boats, or is it paid to the ocean steamship company?
The contract is with the railway company.

Well, Mr. Chairman, that seems to me to be a strange thing. They are two separate corporations. Sir George McL. Brown is in charge in London of the steamship service, and Sir Edward Beatty is in charge at Montreal of the railways. We pay $250,000 of a subsidy. Is that paid to the railway or is it paid to the ocean steamship company?
It is paid to the railway.
Well, I do not know of any railway in Canada that is subsidized.
Sixty millions to the Canadian Pacific Railway.

That is a small figure. They must have got on the inside. I am only asking for information as to what subsidy is paid to the Canadian Pacific Ocean Steamships Limited, which is a separate corporate entity, on their Atlantic service.
I am informed that they are the operating agents of the steamships for the Canadian Pacific Railway, and that is why the money is paid to the Canadian Pacific Railway.

Well, then, I can quite understand why in their report in reference to railways they have written off as depreciation over three and a half million dollars on the ships, and some of their ships are practically new. The Beaver boats are the freight ships, 10,000 tons dead weight capacity, and practically new, about three years old. The Duchess boats are not very old. Only the Mont ships are old'. The Empress of Britain is almost 'new. I find too that they transfer to income acoojumt. what should go to profit and loss account, $2,832,183, and they do not pay any dividend; they say they need that as ready cash in respect of their railways in the United States. I should like to know what amount the department pays for the Atlantic service of the Canadian Pacific Railway and what it pays for the service

Supply-Trade-Mail Subsidies
on the Pacific? The right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) is correct when he says that the Matson Line is obsolete; they have obsolete boats.
No, no, not the Matson.

The Matson line is an
American line.
I know, but the boats are obsolete.
No; they have new boats now.

Then I congratulate them. I think the two ships that are operated by the Canadian Pacific alternate; I believe they run one trip from Vancouver and the other trip from San Francisco. I think that is correct.
No.
Perhaps the ex-Minister of Trade and Commerce can tell us that.
Both from Vancouver.
Does the Aorangi not go from San Francisco, and did the other one, that was lost, not also alternate with San Francisco?
No.
What ships go from San Francisco?
None of the ships involved in these subventions.
Then I should like to know the amount paid to the Canadian Pacific, whether it is to the ocean steamship company or to the railway company, for the Atlantic service. Is it or is it not $250,000?
We pay $250,000 to the Canadian Pacific for their Atlantic service.
And what about the service to Japan?
The service to Japan costs us $600,000, reduced from $749,000.
That is a total of $850,000?
Yes.
Carried.

What is earned, the amount? I was going to suggest to the minister and the government that there is upon the statute books something we have been discussing lately. I refer to the Canadian Pacific-Cana-dian National act, which was passed in order to cut out duplication and pool interests. Why is it that the Canadian Pacific are not asked to have every alternate boat on their Atlantic service turn at Halifax and the other one turn at Saint John?
Mr. EULER; They all call there.

That is like knocking at a door and going away before the people can open the door and speak to you. The point is that if there is to be a pooling of interests it should be a genuine one. We are paying $250,000 for that service, and the freight boats go direct to Saint John. They are unloaded there, and remain in that port a week. Then 'they come around to Halifax, pick up the Canadian National freight there and go off to London. The passenger boats call at Halifax, land the mails and passengers, go around to Saint John, stay .there a week, load up, come back to Halifax, pick up any Canadian National freight that may be there, and go off to Liverpool. I am suggesting that in the interests of the development of the two Atlantic ports, Saint John and Halifax, the boats should call at each port alternately. That is what they do at Montreal and Quebec. The Empress of Britain does not go to Montreal but goes only as far as Quebec. The other boats go to Montreal and then call at Quebec. Is there any sound reason why the boats should not alternate between the Atlantic ports and why the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the government should not take into consideration pooling these interests on the Atlantic coast? Prior to the retirement of Sir Henry Thornton an agreement was entered into and a subsidy was paid the Cunard-White Star line. They called at Halifax and worked up a freight business which inured to the benefit of the Canadian National system to the extent of four or five thousand tons of freight every week. Now *that business is all lost. A great deal of money has been spent in the port of Halifax; I think when the right hon. leader of the opposition returned from England last year he opened a new pier costing $500,000, which is large enough to hold the Queen Mary and two or three other large ships at the same time. Here we are, paying subsidies of $250,000, and I do not think there should be any discrimination as between the two Atlantic ports, Saint John and Halifax, any more than there should be discrimination between Montreal and Quebec.
I should like to ask the minister whether, since he has been in office, he has discussed with the Canadian Pacific the possibility of having each alternate boat turn at Halifax. I am sure that if the subsidy of $250,000 were to be cut in .two and one-half given the White Star line they would call at Halifax every week and 'the Canadian Pacific could call at Saint John, as they do now. Saint John is their terminus; Halifax is not. Halifax is just a port of call, in order to pick up what

Supply-Trade-Mail Subsidies
other ships do not take. I think the two ports should be on a parity, at least in regard to those lines that are subsidized by the government, particularly in view of the act providing for the pooling of interests. They pool on land but they do not seem to pool on sea, and after all that is the right sort of pooling. The water makes the pool there, whereas the only water you get on land is the water that goes into stocks. The minister may not be prepared to answer my question to-night. I do not desire to hold up the estimates or to delay the business of the house
I shall be very glad to give consideration to the representations of the hon. gentleman.
And to bring them to the attention of the government?
Yes.
I should like to support my jolleague from Halifax-

I should like some information in regard to the service between Baddeck and Iona. Are there any ports of call stipulated in the contract, between these two ports?

The contract reads:
Baddeck, Iona or Shenacadie, and MacKay's Point; calling at Kempt Head on the western end of Boularderie island on trips from Baddeck to Iona; such calls to be made on only those days on which the subsidized steamer from Sydney to Whycocomagh makes her westbound trip from Sydney to Whycocomagh; and calling at Grand Narrows whenever there is a reasonable amount of freight or automobiles to put on or take off at that place.
(a) Provided, however, that if weather conditions prevent the steamer making a landing at Iona at any time, she shall, if possible, proceed to Shenacadie to land and take on passengers and freight.
Note: Connections at Iona: the steamer must make connections at Iona with the afternoon eastbound train from Halifax to Sydney from April 1st to November 30th, in each year.

I should like to support the suggestion of my hon. friend from Halifax in connection wibh the port of call of the Canadian Pacific ships. It is true that the subsidy was reduced last year from $500,000 to $250,000. The contract ran out, if I remember rightly, on March 31, 1936, so that it is not this year's but future contracts which I should like to have the minister bear in mind. I do not know whether there is a clause in the contract as to calling at any particular port or ports, but I think the

matter should be seriously considered and a clause inserted, if necessary, to the effect that calls should be made at both Saint John and Halifax on the Atlantic coast with the same amount of time spent in each. As already pointed out by my colleague, a direct benefit is to be gained by the Atlantic ports the same as in regard to boats operating out of Vancouver, where a large amount, $600,000, is paid in subsidies. I support my colleague in his contention; it is something that the minister would be well advised to consider in the future.

I should like to direct the minister's attention to the item on page 38 of the estimates:
Sydney and Bras d'Or lake ports and west coast of Cape Breton and Prince Edward Island, service between, $22,500.
Who is operating that service now?

The contractors are the
Straits Shipping and Contracting Company, Limited, of Sydney, Nova Scotia.

I do not have it before
me, but I am informed that the terms were about the same as this one.

As to
the period or as to the amount?
Mr. ElULER: From 1932 to 1934 the subsidy was $21,225. For 1934-35 it was $20,000; for 1935-36 it was $22,500, and for this year it will be $22,500.

For one season?

Yes.
